sentences.text: The holotype of Limusaurus, the specimen the species is based on, is estimated to be about 1.7 meters long and weigh 15 kilograms.
One adult specimen of Limusaurus is estimated to be 15% larger than the holotype.
Limusaurus had an elongated neck with long cervical vertebrae similar to Elaphrosaurus.
The scapula of Limusaurus had a distinctive prominent ridge at its front edge.
The species Limusaurus inextricabilis was described in 2009 from fossils found in the Upper Shishugou Formation in the Junggar Basin of China.
Limusaurus inextricabilis was named and described in 2009 by paleontologist Xu Xing and colleagues.
The name Limusaurus inextricabilis means "impossible to extricate mud lizard," referring to the hypothesis that the specimens died after being mired in mud.
Seventeen additional specimens of Limusaurus were described in 2017 by Shuo Wang and colleagues from the same excavation blocks as the original 2009 discovery.
Limusaurus underwent a drastic transformation as it aged, losing its juvenile teeth and replacing them with a beak in adulthood.
The loss of teeth in adult Limusaurus likely indicated a dietary shift from omnivory to herbivory, supported by the presence of gastroliths in adults.
Wang and colleagues studied Limusaurus in 2017 to analyze extreme anatomical changes that occurred with growth.
Juvenile Limusaurus specimens grouped separately from adults, indicating significant anatomical changes through growth.
Limusaurus was the first known Ceratosaurian from Asia and belongs to the family Noasauridae, closely related to Elaphrosaurus.
Xu and colleagues classified Limusaurus as a basal member of Ceratosauria in 2009.
A 2016 study by Rauhut and Carrano placed Limusaurus within the abelisauroid family Noasauridae.
Baiano and colleagues found in 2020 that Limusaurus formed a clade with Elaphrosaurus and Huinculsaurus.
Limusaurus lived during the Oxfordian stage of the Jurassic period, approximately 161 to 157 million years ago.
Limusaurus fossils are found in the Shishugou Formation, which dates to the Late Jurassic, approximately 161 to 157 million years ago.
Limusaurus inhabited diverse environments within the Shishugou Formation, including alluvial fans, plains, streams, wetlands, and shallow lakes.
The climate during the time of Limusaurus was likely highly seasonal with warm, wet summers and dry winters due to monsoonal influences.
While Limusaurus may have had feathers, there is no direct evidence for this, though it has sometimes been depicted with them.
A 2010 study by Ezcurra and colleagues debated placing Limusaurus in the derived group Abelisauroidea within Ceratosauria.
Researchers initially used Limusaurus to support the Bilateral Digit Reduction hypothesis regarding theropod hand evolution.
A 2016 analysis suggests the digit reduction in Limusaurus was a developmental anomaly specific to ceratosaurians rather than a pattern shared with tetanurans.
